title: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Blind cave animals of America should be most closely allied to other inhabitants of America, and those of Europe to inhabitants of Europe, rather than the cave faunas of the two continents being specially similar to each other.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Notwithstanding such modifications, we might expect still to see in the cave-animals of America, affinities to the other inhabitants of that continent, and in those of Europe, to the inhabitants of the European continent.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.”. Scope: cave faunas of North America and Europe

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-06: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.89

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is a direct phylogeographic comparison and abundant public sequence and occurrence records exist. Standard phylogenetic analyses can resolve it across many independent cave clades within weeks.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Build phylogenies containing cave and nearby surface taxa from North America and Europe, and compare whether cave species cluster by continent or cave habitat. Repeated sister relationships to same-continent surface lineages support the prediction; a transcontinental cave clade would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Taxonomic sampling differs between continents.

Some cave taxa lack sequence data or reliable locality metadata.

fields.label: Dimension scores

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is a tree topology with a clear alternative, and sequences plus synthesized trees already cover the American and European faunas named in the scope. A team can assemble clade-by-clade tests with standard phylogenetic methods in weeks to a couple of months. Incomplete sampling would widen confidence intervals; it would not change the contrast between regional nesting and a special cave-to-cave relationship.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Assemble phylogenies of cave and surface relatives for North American and European clades. Nesting of cave species inside the surface fauna of the same continent would confirm the prediction; clades that unite American and European cave species apart from their local surface relatives would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Introductions and long-distance subterranean dispersal can create transcontinental relatives.

Published trees differ in markers and species sampling and need a common rooting.

Some invertebrate cave groups are still sparsely sequenced.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.88
analysis feasibility: 0.76
discriminating power: 0.82
data existence: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.7

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: In a phylogeny containing obligate cave (troglobitic/stygobitic) animals and surface animals from North America and Europe, each cave lineage is nested among, or sister to, taxa of its own continent; American and European cave taxa do not form clades with each other to the exclusion of surface taxa.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: 81 pre-registered species (40 obligate cave, 41 surface; 5 groups) were matched to Open Tree taxonomy with the TNRS (1 unmatched: Neaphaenops tellkampfi), and their continent was checked against GBIF occurrence counts in North America vs Europe (1 dropped: Crangonyx pseudogracilis, now mostly recorded in Europe where it is introduced). The induced subtree of synthetic tree opentree16.1 was requested for the remaining 79 taxa. For each of the 38 cave taxa the node-count distance to the nearest same-continent taxon and to the nearest other-continent cave taxon was computed, and all clades were scanned for ones containing cave taxa of both continents but no surface taxon.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Using the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree induced on the taxa listed in derived/taxa.csv (continent assignment verified with GBIF occurrences), for every cave taxon compute the node-count distance to the nearest same-continent taxon (cave or surface, d_same) and to the nearest other-continent cave taxon (d_othercave). The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) d_same <= d_othercave for at least 70% of cave taxa, and (ii) the induced tree contains no clade that includes at least one North American and at least one European cave taxon while containing no surface taxon ('exclusive transcontinental cave clade').

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if fewer than 50% of cave taxa satisfy d_same <= d_othercave, or if two or more independent exclusive transcontinental cave clades occur (in different taxonomic groups). Results between the two thresholds, or a single such clade, are recorded as 'mixed'. If fewer than 10 cave taxa (across at least 3 groups) can be placed in the tree, the verdict is inconclusive/underpowered.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of cave taxa with nearest same-continent taxon at least as close as nearest other-continent cave taxon

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'cave-animals of America' and 'of Europe' are read as obligate subterranean species of North America and Europe; 'affinities to the other inhabitants of that continent' is read as phylogenetic relationship (sister-group or nesting) to surface lineages of the same continent, versus the alternative he rejects, that the two continents' cave faunas are specially allied to each other. Taxa were chosen before any tree was inspected and are listed in derived/taxa.csv; groups are Amphibia (Urodela), Amphipoda, Isopoda, Coleoptera (Trechini and Leiodidae) and Orthoptera (Rhaphidophoridae), the groups in which both continents have well-known troglobites. Continent assignment of each species is verified post hoc against GBIF: a species is kept only if at least 90% of its GBIF occurrences on the two continents fall on the pre-registered continent; names that the Open Tree TNRS cannot match are dropped. Phylogenetic 'affinity' is measured by node counts on the synthetic tree because it has no branch lengths; polytomies produce ties, which count in favour of whichever criterion they satisfy (a tie between a same-continent and an other-continent cave neighbour satisfies d_same <= d_othercave).

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Open Tree of Life synthetic tree (current version via API v3)

GBIF occurrence search API (continent facet)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The synthetic tree has no branch lengths and several groups are poorly resolved (Asellidae genera, Niphargus/Crangonyctidae, Cholevinae), so node-count distances are coarse; both failing cases (Monolistra caeca, Ptomaphagus hirtus) arise where the induced tree places same-continent relatives in a deeper or unresolved position, and Ptomaphagus hirtus sits in a Staphylinoidea polytomy with the European Leptodirini.

The surface comparators are a pre-registered selection, not an exhaustive sample of each continent's fauna; adding taxa could only shorten d_same, so the design is lenient toward the claim in that respect, but the second criterion (no exclusive transcontinental cave clade) does not depend on how many surface taxa were sampled within the included families.

Proteus anguinus (Europe) is sister to Necturus (North America, surface) in the tree: a transatlantic family-level link that is not a cave-to-cave link; d_same for Proteus is the distance to European Salamandridae.

No European obligate cave fishes were available, so Amblyopsidae were not included; the cross-continent comparison therefore covers salamanders, amphipods, isopods, beetles and cave crickets only.

Open Tree synthesis is itself built from published phylogenies plus taxonomy, so this is a test against the current synthesis of the literature rather than a de novo molecular analysis.
